items.stem: A software company in Bogotá introduces a bonus for every bug fixed. Programmers who used to enjoy fixing difficult bugs now only fix easy ones. (a) Suggest an alternative reward system and explain why it might be better. (b) Suggest one non-monetary way of increasing intrinsic motivation.
items.answer: (a) Profit-sharing or recognition for solving difficult problems, so reward is not tied to the number of bugs and challenge is valued. (b) Give programmers autonomy to choose interesting projects, or time for creative work.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark system; 1 mark reason [2] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: Evaluate the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia, including a discussion of negative symptoms.
items.answer: Strength (supporting evidence): Antipsychotic drugs that block D2 receptors reduce positive symptoms, and amphetamines that raise dopamine can cause psychosis, supporting a role for dopamine. Strength (usefulness): It led to the development of antipsychotic drugs that allow many patients to live in the community. Weakness (negative symptoms): It explains positive symptoms better than negative symptoms, which respond poorly to dopamine-blocking drugs. Weakness (cause and effect): Raised dopamine activity could be a result of the disorder or of stress rather than its cause. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Grace showed 10 children in Dhaka a film clip in which a brand of cola appeared and 10 children the same clip with the brand removed. Afterwards each child chose a drink, and the number choosing that brand over five occasions was recorded. Table: Times the brand was chosen (out of 5) — Placement clip: 2, 0, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 2, 3, 3. No-placement clip: 1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 3, 0, 4, 1, 1. (a) Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place. (b) Explain why the median may be a better measure of central tendency than the mean for the placement clip condition. (c) Name a suitable type of graph to display the mean scores for the two conditions, and justify your choice. (d) The participants were students whose names were drawn at random from a list of every student at a college in Dhaka. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it.
items.answer: (a) Placement clip: 2.6; no-placement clip: 1.6. (b) The score of 0 is an extreme score (outlier) compared with the rest of the placement clip data; the mean is distorted by it, but the median is not affected by extreme values, so it is more representative. (c) Bar chart, because the IV has separate (discrete) categories, so the mean for each condition is shown as a separate bar with gaps between bars. (d) Random sampling. Weakness: it needs a complete list of the target population and selected people may refuse, so the final sample may still be unrepresentative.
items.markingKey: (a) Placement clip: 26 ÷ 10 = 2.6; no-placement clip: 16 ÷ 10 = 1.6. 1 mark for each correct mean [2] (b) 1 mark: identifies the outlier (0); 1 mark: mean distorted / median unaffected by extreme scores [2] (c) 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: justification (discrete conditions / categories, not continuous data) [2] (d) 1 mark: sampling technique; 1 mark: weakness explained [2]

items.stem: ‘Restaurant design has a greater influence on diners than the food itself.’ To what extent do you agree? In your answer, you may refer to individual differences and ecological validity.
items.answer: Arguments for: Menu layout, descriptive labels and price format influence what diners choose and spend. Seating and table spacing affect comfort and satisfaction. Atmosphere (music, lighting, scent) affects mood and time spent. Arguments against: Diners return mainly because of food quality and price. Many studies have small effects and use limited samples. Cultural differences in personal space and dining habits limit generalisation. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how cognitive biases can maintain gambling. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “Operant conditioning cannot explain why people continue to gamble after losing.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Gamblers may believe they have skill or control (illusion of control), see near misses as nearly winning, or think a win is “due” (gambler’s fallacy), so they continue despite losses. (b) Not correct. Variable-ratio reinforcement and near misses explain persistence despite losses.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark named bias; 1 mark how it maintains gambling [2] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Design an observation to investigate how often adverts aimed at children are shown during children’s programmes. Your plan must include: how inter-rater reliability will be checked, ethical issues and behavioural categories.
items.answer: Method: an observation. Structured observation with operationalised behavioural categories and time sampling; two observers to check inter-rater reliability; overt or covert as appropriate. Variables: behaviour: adverts shown; categories: food, toys, games, other. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Seoul, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.

items.stem: Arjun measured the number of errors made in a data-entry task by 9 employees in Muscat working in a quiet private office and 9 employees in a noisy open-plan office. Table: Errors per hour — Private office: 8, 7, 7, 3, 11, 9, 8, 9, 9. Open-plan office: 10, 40, 15, 14, 7, 12, 10, 16, 9. (a) Write a non-directional (two-tailed) hypothesis for this study. (b) Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results. (c) The standard deviation for the private office condition was 2.20 and for the open-plan office condition was 9.91. Explain what these values show. (d) Explain one ethical issue that the researcher should consider in this study.
items.answer: (a) There will be a difference in the number of errors between employees in private offices and employees in open-plan offices. (b) The open-plan office condition had a higher mean (14.8) than the private office condition (7.9), suggesting that private offices increase errors. (c) The open-plan office condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent. (d) Results should not be used to discipline individuals.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV and DV both included (operationalised); 1 mark: correct form of hypothesis [2] (b) 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2] (c) 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2] (d) 1 mark: ethical guideline named; 1 mark: applied to this study [2]

items.stem: Sipho, a teacher in Singapore, suffers from tension headaches and a racing heart before school inspections. (a) Suggest how biofeedback could help Sipho. (b) Explain why SIT might be better for Sipho in the long term.
items.answer: (a) Use EMG sensors on the forehead to show muscle tension; Sipho practises relaxation until tension drops, learning to relax without the equipment. (b) It teaches coping skills for future inspections and other stressors without side effects or dependence.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark sensors/feedback; 1 mark learned control [2] (b) 1 mark skills; 1 mark no side effects [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “Daily hassles may be a better predictor of stress than major life events.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe the general adaptation syndrome.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Research such as Kanner et al. found hassles related strongly to psychological symptoms. (b) Alarm: the stressor is detected and the sympathetic system and adrenaline produce fight or flight. Resistance: the body adapts and maintains high arousal with cortisol. Exhaustion: with continued stress, resources are depleted and stress-related illness may develop.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each stage [3]

items.answer: (a) Not correct. Grid layouts are easiest for finding items; freeform layouts encourage browsing. (b) The loop path exposes customers to every department, so they see more products and are more likely to make unplanned purchases.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark exposure; 1 mark impulse purchases [2]

items.stem: A register study in Auckland followed children of parents with and without schizophrenia into adulthood. Children with both parents with schizophrenia: 278 followed up, 80 diagnosed with schizophrenia. Children with one parent with schizophrenia: 1177 followed up, 87 diagnosed with schizophrenia. Children with neither parent with schizophrenia: 25620 followed up, 178 diagnosed with schizophrenia. (a) Calculate the percentage of children with neither parent with schizophrenia who were diagnosed with schizophrenia. Give your answer to one decimal place. (b) Explain what these data suggest about genetic factors in schizophrenia. (c) Explain why these data cannot prove that schizophrenia is caused by genes. (d) Suggest one other type of study that could separate genetic and environmental influences.
items.answer: (a) 0.7% (b) Risk rises as the number of affected parents rises, which is consistent with a genetic contribution. (c) Children usually live with their parents, so they share environment as well as genes (for example stress of living with an unwell parent), and most children of affected parents do not develop schizophrenia. (d) An adoption study comparing adopted children of parents with schizophrenia with adopted children of unaffected parents, or a comparison of MZ and DZ twins.
items.markingKey: (a) 178 ÷ 25620 × 100 = 0.7%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 1 mark pattern; 1 mark genetic interpretation [2] (c) 1 mark shared environment; 1 mark most do not develop it [2] (d) 1 mark study type; 1 mark how it separates influences [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why doctors may make more type I than type II errors. (b) Describe Safer et al.’s three stages of delay in seeking treatment.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why shift work can affect health and safety. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “Rotating shift workers may be at greater risk of accidents than fixed-shift workers.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.

items.stem: Mei and Omar work in a hospital in Muscat. Both want the same week of holiday, and only one can be absent. Mei insists, while Omar says nothing and lets Mei have the week, but is now resentful. (a) Identify the conflict modes used by Mei and Omar. (b) Suggest how the manager could help them collaborate.
items.answer: (a) Mei: competing; Omar: accommodating. (b) Meet both, explore underlying needs (for example one needs travel dates, the other a family event) and find a solution such as splitting weeks or finding cover.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark exploring needs; 1 mark win–win solution [2]

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which systematic desensitisation is the most effective treatment for phobias.
items.answer: Arguments for: It is gradual, so it is ethical and acceptable to patients. Many studies show it reduces fear of specific objects. Arguments against: Flooding can work more quickly. Applied tension is more suitable for blood-injection-injury phobia because of fainting. Some patients cannot imagine scenes or learn relaxation. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “The theory that pain is a direct response from specific pain receptors, with the amount of pain proportional to the injury”?
items.answer: Specificity theory
items.markingKey: Specificity theory: the theory that pain is a direct response from specific pain receptors, with the amount of pain proportional to the injury. [1]

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “Rewarding patients for following medical advice to increase future adherence”.
items.answer: Positive reinforcement for adherence
items.markingKey: Positive reinforcement for adherence: rewarding patients for following medical advice to increase future adherence. [1]

items.stem: With reference to physiological measures of stress (such as GSR, heart rate and cortisol), explain one weakness relating to validity.
items.answer: Arousal can be caused by excitement or exercise, so high readings do not always mean stress.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to validity; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A restaurant in Bogotá tested two menu designs. On 8 evenings the menu showed prices with a currency symbol and on 8 evenings prices were shown as plain numbers. Average spending per diner was recorded. Table: Average spend per diner ($) — Plain numbers: 37, 40, 35, 42, 33, 38, 40, 30. With currency symbol: 29, 32, 34, 31, 29, 36, 29, 33. What is the range of scores for the with currency symbol condition?
Outline one strength of Fiedler’s contingency theory of leadership that relates to situational factors.
items.answer: It recognises that no single style is best, so it explains why leaders succeed in one role but fail in another.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to situational factors; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Sipho, aged 7, in Lima, was bitten by a dog at a park. Since then Sipho screams at the sight of any dog, even small ones on television. Use classical conditioning to explain how Sipho’s fear developed.
items.answer: The dog (neutral stimulus) was paired with the pain of the bite (UCS → fear UCR), so dogs became a conditioned stimulus producing fear (CR).
items.markingKey: 1 mark pairing; 1 mark CS → CR [2]

items.stem: Outline one strength of Fox et al.’s (1987) token economy for mine safety that relates to usefulness.
items.answer: It reduced injuries and saved money, so other industries could adopt similar schemes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to usefulness; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Ana, from Lisbon, noticed a lump three months ago but has only just visited a doctor. Ana says: “At first I thought it was nothing, then I meant to book an appointment but kept putting it off.” (a) Suggest one reason for each type of delay. (b) Suggest how health services could reduce such delays.
items.answer: (a) Appraisal: no pain, so the symptom seemed unimportant. Utilisation: fear of a serious diagnosis or practical problems such as work. (b) Public campaigns about warning signs and easier, faster appointment systems.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: ‘Psychological treatments are more effective than drug treatments for impulse control disorders.’ Evaluate this statement, using evidence from psychology. In your answer, you may refer to effectiveness and case studies.
items.answer: Arguments for: Imaginal desensitisation and covert sensitisation target the learned urge and teach control. Case studies (for example Glover, 2011) report long-lasting improvement. Arguments against: Naltrexone reduces urges in many patients in controlled trials. Evidence for psychological treatments often comes from small samples or single cases. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Jonas compared Y-BOCS scores after 12 weeks for clients randomly allocated to ERP or relaxation training. Table: Y-BOCS score after 12 weeks — ERP: 11, 20, 21, 12, 16, 14, 19, 18. Relaxation training: 19, 17, 23, 26, 24, 24, 25, 18. (a) Calculate the median score for the ERP condition. (b) Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results. (c) The standard deviation for the ERP condition was 3.74 and for the relaxation training condition was 3.46. Explain what these values show. (d) Explain one ethical issue that the researcher should consider in this study.
items.answer: (a) 17 (b) The relaxation training condition had a higher mean (22.0) than the ERP condition (16.4), suggesting that ERP reduces OCD symptoms more than relaxation training. (c) The ERP condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent. (d) The relaxation group should be offered ERP afterwards.
items.markingKey: (a) Ordered scores: 11, 12, 14, 16, 18, 19, 20, 21; median = 17. 1 mark: data ordered; 1 mark: correct median [2] (b) 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2] (c) 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2] (d) 1 mark: ethical guideline named; 1 mark: applied to this study [2]

items.stem: A café owner in Riyadh, Amara, wants customers to stay longer at lunchtime on quiet days but leave more quickly on busy days. (a) Suggest how Amara could use music on busy days and explain why. (b) Explain one ethical issue in using music to influence customers.
items.answer: (a) Play faster music so customers eat more quickly and tables are freed for new customers. (b) Customers are influenced without awareness or consent, which could be seen as manipulation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark fast music; 1 mark effect [2] (b) 1 mark issue; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Kathmandu is interested in whether CBT reduces the distress caused by hallucinations in people with schizophrenia. Design a field experiment to test this. Your plan must include: ethical issues, how the dependent variable will be measured and controls.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: CBT or usual care; DV: distress rating from 0 to 10. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Kathmandu, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “A large shared workspace without walls or private offices”?
items.answer: Open-plan office

items.stem: Explain one weakness of Janis and Feshbach’s (1953) study of fear arousal in terms of generalisability.
items.answer: The sample was from one American high school in the 1950s, so attitudes may differ today and elsewhere.

items.stem: A new bookshop is opening in Mexico City. The owner, Amara, wants customers to stay longer and buy more books on impulse. Recommend a store layout and explain your choice.
items.answer: A freeform layout, with displays of different shapes and themed tables, encourages browsing and impulse buying; or a racetrack that leads customers past all sections.

items.stem: Ana wants to find out whether a short course of CBT reduces negative automatic thoughts in students with low mood. Design a field experiment to investigate this. Your plan must include: how the dependent variable will be measured, controls and the experimental design.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: CBT course or waiting list; DV: number of negative thoughts recorded in a diary. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Santiago, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Ravi set up a tasting stand in a supermarket in Nairobi. On 9 days it showed 24 flavours of jam and on 9 days it showed 6 flavours. The number of jars bought (per 100 visitors to the stand) was recorded each day. Table: Jars bought per 100 visitors — 6 flavours: 21, 20, 20, 16, 20, 17, 21, 22, 22. 24 flavours: 0, 3, 0, 4, 0, 7, 1, 3, 3. (a) Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results. (b) Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here. (c) Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why. (d) Name a suitable type of graph to display the mean scores for the two conditions, and justify your choice.
items.answer: (a) The 6 flavours condition had a higher mean (19.9) than the 24 flavours condition (2.3), suggesting that a smaller choice set leads to more purchases (choice overload). (b) Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV. (c) The same brand and prices of jam on all days. (d) Bar chart, because the IV has separate (discrete) categories, so the mean for each condition is shown as a separate bar with gaps between bars.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2] (b) 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2] (c) 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2] (d) 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: justification (discrete conditions / categories, not continuous data) [2]

items.stem: Ines plays an online slot game in Accra every evening. Ines says: “I nearly won three times today, so a big win is definitely coming.” (a) Explain why near misses encourage Ines to keep playing. (b) Use operant conditioning to explain why the game is difficult to stop playing.
items.answer: (a) Near misses activate the reward system and feel like nearly winning, acting as reinforcement and suggesting skill or that a win is close. (b) Wins occur on a variable-ratio schedule, so behaviour is highly resistant to extinction; each unpredictable win reinforces playing.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reinforcing; 1 mark belief [2] (b) 1 mark VR schedule; 1 mark resistance to extinction [2]

items.stem: Mei, a man with schizophrenia in Muscat, has taken chlorpromazine for five years. His hallucinations are reduced, but he has developed involuntary lip-smacking and rarely leaves his room. (a) Identify the side effect Mei is experiencing. (b) Suggest a different drug treatment and explain one advantage of it. (c) Suggest how a token economy could help Mei with his negative symptoms.
items.answer: (a) Tardive dyskinesia. (b) An atypical antipsychotic such as clozapine, which causes fewer movement side effects and may help negative symptoms. (c) Reward small steps such as leaving his room, washing or joining activities with tokens exchanged for privileges, reinforcing these behaviours.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark drug; 1 mark advantage [2] (c) 1 mark target behaviour; 1 mark reinforcement [2]
